1.pericope_label: I will bless the Lord at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth

schools.summary: Delitzsch dates the psalm among the eight assigned to the persecution by Saul, and treats its closing verse as a deliberate supernumerary letter rather than a displaced one.
Gill opens the resolve to bless upon both providence and grace; Calvin devotes the bulk of his comment to refusing any excuse for the dissimulation while insisting the deliverance was God's.
Clarke does the textual work — the name Abimelech, the missing acrostic letter, the displaced last verse — and rescues David's character by preferring the Greek account of an epileptic fit.

Henry and Spurgeon both refuse to let the occasion spoil the praise — Henry declining to justify the stratagem yet marvelling at the composure that produced the psalm, Spurgeon insisting we must not rob God of honour because conscience censures our share in the transaction.
Augustine leaves the history alone and reads the changed countenance allegorically, of a change in the priesthood and a sacrifice after the order of Melchizedek.

debates.question: Can David's feigned madness be defended?

positions.summary: No: it ill became an honest man to feign himself what he was not, though the composure of spirit that produced the psalm in that fright is still to be wondered at.
No, and emphatically: the intermediate sin is on no account to be excused, and it is a superfluous task to try to exculpate David, who exposed the grace of the Spirit to the derision of the ungodly.
The question does not arise as usually put: the Greek account of an epileptic fit is preferable, and saves David's character — failing which, let it fall under reproach.
The prayer offered in that state must have been confused and full of self-sufficiency, yet it was accepted, which is the more reason to celebrate the mercy.

debates.question: How should the defective acrostic be repaired?

positions.summary: The last verse originally carried the missing letter and belongs after the fifth, as more than a hundred of Kennicott's manuscripts read it.
The closing verse is a deliberate supernumerary letter, matching the same device at the end of an earlier psalm, not a displaced one.

debates.question: Did the Spirit who dictated the psalm suggest the stratagem?

positions.summary: No. God sometimes delivers his people while they err in choosing the means; the deliverance is his work, the sin theirs, as with Rebekah and the blessing.
The escape was providential rather than contrived, God causing the fit that secured his dismissal.

outliers.summary: Reads the title entirely figuratively — the changed countenance as a change of priesthood, the drumming as the Cross, the carrying in his own hands as the institution of the Supper.

themes: I will bless the Lord at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth.

2.pericope_label: My soul shall make her boast in the Lord: the humble shall hear thereof, and be glad... O taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him

schools.summary: Delitzsch and Ellicott work on the verbs and the idiom — the intense seeking, the Aramaic sense of shining derived from flowing — and Ellicott reduces the encamping angel to a general expression for divine protection.
Gill weighs both the uncreated and the created Angel, spreads the goodness to be tasted across the three Persons, and defends the silent prayer offered in the court of Gath.
Clarke makes the angel a watchman on his circuit and the promises the grand test of revelation, any man being able to prove them; Wesley keeps the readings short and plain.
Henry keeps the comfort of angelic ministry without settling its number; Spurgeon presses the experimental point that one cannot see except by tasting.

debates.question: Who or what is the angel of the Lord that encampeth round about?

positions.summary: Either the uncreated Angel of the covenant or a created angel, one being sufficient to destroy an army.
The One who was the medium of God's intercourse with the patriarchs, accompanied by inferior ministering angels, with an allusion to the angel-camp that met Jacob.
A watchman going his circuit, with those who fear the Lord as the objects of his special care.
A general expression for the divine manifestation of protection, which avoids the awkward image of one angel encamped round a single sufferer.
The singular is simply put for the plural.

debates.question: Does the verb rendered 'were lightened' mean shining or flowing?

positions.summary: Enlightened, following the Targum's 'their faces were enlightened', though the alternative sense of flowing to God is reported.
Flowing is the proper sense, shining an Aramaic development of it, as in the reflex of divine glory lighting the face.
Comforted and encouraged, and not disappointed of their hope.

debates.question: Who are the humble who shall hear and be glad?

positions.summary: The afflicted, such as David had been.
Those who have learnt patience in the school of suffering; the Greek and Latin render it the meek.
The righteous.

outliers.summary: Follows several manuscripts and the ancient versions in reading 'the rich' for 'the young lions', and quotes his old Psalter's rendering of the verse.

themes: My soul shall make her boast in the Lord: the humble shall hear thereof, and be glad.
O magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.
I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed.
This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him, and saved him out of all his troubles.
The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
O taste and see that the Lord is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
O fear the Lord, ye his saints: for there is no want to them that fear him.
The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing.

11.pericope_label: Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord... Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it

schools.summary: Delitzsch marks the formal turn to a didactic second division and denies that the children are children in years; Ellicott calls the address a common proverbial style and the sayings echoes from Proverbs.
Gill canvasses every possible sense of 'children' and takes the desired life as running from natural through spiritual to eternal.
Clarke turns the verse into an attack on teaching heathen mythology before sound divinity; Wesley folds the two lives into one and presses the pursuit of peace.
Henry and Spurgeon both dwell on the dignity of teaching the young, Henry on the charity of schooling neglected children, Spurgeon on the art of winning them.

positions.summary: Not children in years or understanding, but a tender form of address from a master experienced in the ways of God.
Any of several: David's family, his subjects, young people generally, or the children of God, particularly the least among them.
Literal children, taught by a king who did not think the work below him, and perhaps especially those whose parents neglect them.
Those of a humble and teachable spirit.

debates.question: What life does the psalm promise to the man who desires it?

positions.summary: Natural, healthful and prosperous life, then spiritual life, and perhaps best of all eternal life.
A long and happy life begun in this world and continued for ever in the next.
It must look beyond the present world, since man's life on earth consists of few days and those full of trouble.
The man delighting in life, in the gnomic manner of Proverbs — earthly and proverbial rather than eschatological.

outliers.summary: Prints his old Psalter's paraphrase — not the fables of poets nor the stories of tyrants but the dread of the Lord — and makes the verse a rebuke to classical education.
Suggests the boys and girls of Gath had made sport of David's feigned madness, so that his teaching here undoes the mischief he had done.

themes: Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord.
What man is he that desireth life, and loveth many days, that he may see good?
Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile.
Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.

15.pericope_label: The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry... The Lord redeemeth the soul of his servants: and none of them that trust in him shall be desolate

schools.summary: Ellicott and Delitzsch handle the alphabet and the prepositions — Ellicott arguing two verses should change places and that the order of two Hebrew letters was never fixed, Delitzsch reading the closing letter as a deliberate repetition.
Gill refers the many afflictions and the unbroken bones first to Christ, and reads the redemption of the soul as the continual application of what was purchased.

Clarke supplies the missing word 'righteous', draws out the hammer behind the broken heart and the contrite spirit, and reads the last word as guilty rather than desolate; Wesley keeps to short glosses.
Spurgeon presses the intentness of the divine attention and the deliberateness of the divine opposition.

debates.question: Is the promise of unbroken bones about Christ or about believers generally?

positions.summary: Best understood of Christ throughout, since the bones of many martyrs were broken on the rack and wheel, and a general reading would distress anyone who suffers such an accident.
General and untroubled: God takes care of his life, and if he has scars they are honourable ones.
Points simply to the fulfilment recorded in John.

debates.question: Is the acrostic order at these verses disturbed?

positions.summary: Yes: the sense requires two verses to change places, and the same irregular sequence in Lamentations shows the order of those two letters was not invariably fixed.
No: the alphabet is complete, and what follows is a deliberate supernumerary letter matching an earlier psalm.

debates.question: What does the last word of the psalm mean?

positions.summary: Not desolate but guilty, so that the servants are preserved from sin and forfeit neither life nor soul.
Better rendered found guilty, or condemned.
The forgiveness, justification and sanctification continually applied to the servants of God.

outliers.summary: Reads the broken heart and contrite spirit as metal-working terms — shivered ore and beaten-out metal — with the hammer necessarily implied, and makes the two the essential marks of true repentance.

themes: The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry.
The face of the Lord is against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth.
The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.
The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the Lord delivereth him out of them all.
He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken.
Evil shall slay the wicked: and they that hate the righteous shall be desolate.
The Lord redeemeth the soul of his servants: and none of them that trust in him shall be desolate.
